title: Statistics
short: Mean, median and mode of grouped data, and ogives.
lede: A table plus three methods for the mean. Almost entirely mechanical, which makes it very scoring.
lens: Most of the **11-mark Statistics and Probability unit**, roughly **7–8 marks**.
Almost always one 4–5 mark question: find the mean, median or mode of grouped data, or find a missing frequency f.
The step-deviation method is the fastest and is accepted for the mean.
concepts: **1. Grouped data.** Data arranged in class intervals with frequencies. For calculations, each class is represented by its **class mark** `xᵢ = (upper limit + lower limit)/2`.
**2. Three methods for the mean.** Direct method, assumed-mean method and step-deviation method. All three give the same answer — use whichever suits the numbers.

head: Method
Formula
rows: x̄ = a + (Σfᵢdᵢ / Σfᵢ), where dᵢ = xᵢ − a
x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h, where uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h

concepts: **3. Median of grouped data.** `Median = l + [((N/2 − cf)/f) × h]`, where l is the lower limit of the **median class**, N = Σfᵢ, cf is the cumulative frequency of the class *before* the median class, f is the frequency of the median class and h is the class width.
**4. Finding the median class.** Compute N/2 and find the class whose cumulative frequency is the first one **greater than** N/2.

**5. Mode of grouped data.** `Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h`, where l is the lower limit of the **modal class** (highest frequency), f₁ its frequency, f₀ the frequency of the preceding class and f₂ of the following class.
**6. Empirical relationship.** `3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean`. Handy for checking your answers when all three are asked.

**7. Ogives.** A **less than** ogive plots the upper class limits against the less-than cumulative frequencies. A **more than** ogive plots the lower limits against more-than cumulative frequencies. The x-coordinate where the two curves intersect is the **median**.
formulas: Step deviation: x̄ = a + (Σfᵢuᵢ / Σfᵢ) × h
Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h
steps: 1. Add a class-mark column (xᵢ) and a cumulative-frequency column (cf) before you start any calculation.
2. For the mean, pick a as a class mark near the middle so the deviations are small.
3. For the median, compute N/2 first and identify the median class from the cf column.
4. For the mode, identify the modal class from the **frequency** column, not the cumulative one.
5. Check with 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean if you have computed all three.
tricks: - **Median class vs modal class are different things.** Median comes from the cumulative frequency crossing N/2; mode comes from the largest frequency.
- **cf in the median formula is the cumulative frequency of the class *before* the median class.** Using the median class’s own cf is the single most common error here.
- Choose a = a class mark (not a class limit) for the assumed mean, and h = the class width.
- If a class is written as “10–20, 20–30”, the boundary value 20 belongs to the later class.
- For a missing frequency f, use Σfᵢ = N and the mean formula together to get two equations.
mistakes: - Using class limits instead of class marks in the mean.
- Using the wrong cf in the median formula.
- In the mode formula, taking f₀ and f₂ from the wrong side.
- Forgetting to multiply by h at the end of the step-deviation and mode formulas.
- Drawing an ogive with class marks on the x-axis. Ogives use class **limits**.

qa.q: Find the class mark of the class 25–35.
qa.a: The class mark is the midpoint of the class: (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2 = (25 + 35)/2 = **30**. It stands in for every value in that interval when a mean is calculated from grouped data, which is why it is also called the mid-value.

qa.q: Write the formula for the mode of grouped data and explain each symbol.
qa.a: Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h, where l is the lower limit of the modal class, f₁ its frequency, f₀ the frequency of the class before it, f₂ the frequency of the class after it, and h the class size. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency.

qa.q: Find the mean of the data: class intervals 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 with frequencies 3, 5, 7, 5.
Find the mode of the data: 10–20 (f = 3), 20–30 (f = 12), 30–40 (f = 9).
A student finds the mean of the data 0–10 (f = 4) and 10–20 (f = 6) using the upper limits 10 and 20 as x. Find the error, and give the correct mean.
a: Error: for grouped data, x must be the **class mark** (the midpoint of the class), not a class limit.
Class marks are 5 and 15, so the mean = (4 × 5 + 6 × 15)/(4 + 6) = (20 + 90)/10.
Mean = **11**. The upper-limit method would have wrongly given (40 + 120)/10 = 16.

qa.q: The daily wages of 40 workers are: Rs 100–200: 8, 200–300: 12, 300–400: 10, 400–500: 6, 500–600: 4. Form the “more than” cumulative frequency table and find how many workers earn Rs 400 or more.
a: A “more than” table lists the number of workers with wages at or above each lower limit.
More than 100: 40; more than 200: 32; more than 300: 20; more than 400: 10; more than 500: 4.

qa.q: Find the median of the distribution: 0–10 (f = 4), 10–20 (f = 6), 20–30 (f = 10), 30–40 (f = 8), 40–50 (f = 2).
a: Cumulative frequencies: 4, 10, 20, 28, 30. So N = 30 and N/2 = 15.
The first cf greater than 15 is 20, so the median class is 20–30.

qa.q: The mean of the distribution 0–10 (f = 5), 10–20 (f = f), 20–30 (f = 8), 30–40 (f = 7) is 20.5. Find f.
a: 15f + 470 = 20.5f + 410, so 5.5f = 60 and f ≈ 10.9. Check your reading of the data — frequencies must be whole numbers, so re-check the given mean before answering.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

The weekly hours of study of 40 students are: 0–10: 5 students, 10–20: 8, 20–30: 14, 30–40: 9, 40–50: 4.

(a) Write the class marks.
(b) Find the mean.
(c) Which is the modal class, and why?
a: (c) The modal class is **20–30**, because it has the highest frequency (14).

qa.q:
Read and answer:

In a survey, the mean daily screen time of students is 3.4 hours and the median is 3.2 hours.

(a) Find the mode using the empirical relation.
(b) What does the order mean > median > mode suggest about the data?
(c) Which measure would you report if a few students have extremely long screen times, and why?
a: (b) The data are skewed to the right: a few large values pull the mean above the median and mode.
(c) The median, because it is not affected by extreme values, while the mean is.

qa.q: Find the mean of this data by the step-deviation method: 0–20 (f = 7), 20–40 (f = 12), 40–60 (f = 16), 60–80 (f = 13), 80–100 (f = 12).
For the distribution 0–10 (5), 10–20 (8), 20–30 (12), 30–40 (7), 40–50 (3), write the less-than cumulative frequencies, name the median class and find the median.
a: Less-than cumulative frequencies: 5, 13, 25, 32, 35. N = 35, so N/2 = 17.5.
The cumulative frequency first crosses 17.5 in the class 20–30, so that is the median class.

mcq.q: The class mark of the class 15–25 is: (a) 15  (b) 25  (c) 10  (d) 20
The median class is the class whose cumulative frequency is: (a) the first one greater than N/2  (b) equal to N/2  (c) the largest  (d) the smallest
mcq.a: **(a) The first one greater than N/2.**

mcq.q: If mean = 20 and mode = 26, then by the empirical relation the median is: (a) 22  (b) 22.67  (c) 23  (d) 24

In grouped data, the mean is calculated using the class marks because: (a) the class limits are never known  (b) it always makes the mean larger  (c) the frequencies are not required  (d) every observation of a class is assumed to lie at its midpoint
mcq.a: **(d) every observation of a class is assumed to lie at its midpoint.** The individual values inside a class are unknown, so each is represented by the class mark.

mcq.q: In the mode formula l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h, the symbol f₁ stands for: (a) the frequency of the class before the modal class  (b) the frequency of the class after the modal class  (c) the frequency of the modal class  (d) the total of all frequencies
mcq.a: **(c) the frequency of the modal class.** f₁ is the frequency of the modal class; f₀ and f₂ are those of the classes just before and just after it.
**(b) 5.** It occurs three times, more than any other value.

mcq.q: The class mark of the class 45–55 is: (a) 100  (b) 55  (c) 50  (d) 45
The empirical relation connecting the three measures of central tendency is: (a) Median = 3 Mode − 2 Mean  (b) Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean  (c) Mean = 3 Median − 2 Mode  (d) Mode = 2 Median − Mean
mcq.a: **(b) Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean.** Equivalently, 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.

trend: One 4–5 mark grouped-data question every year — mean, median, mode or a missing frequency. Ogive drawing is asked less often now but still appears in sample papers.
onepager: - Use class marks, not class limits.
- Median: cf is the cumulative frequency **before** the median class.
- Mode uses the frequency column, not the cf column.
- 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean as a check.
task: Build a grouped frequency table from 30 real measurements (heights of people in your building, leaf lengths, anything). Then find the mean by all three methods and confirm they agree.

title: Probability
short: Classical probability, complementary events, dice, cards and coins.
lede: The shortest chapter in the book and among the most certain marks.
lens: The remaining **3–4 marks of the 11-mark unit**.
Almost always one 2–3 mark question on a die, a pair of dice, a deck of cards or coloured balls.
The CBSE syllabus restricts this to the classical definition and simple single-event problems. No two-event multiplication rules.
concepts: **1. Classical definition.** `P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of possible outcomes)`, assuming all outcomes are equally likely.
**2. Range.** `0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1`. An impossible event has probability 0; a certain event has probability 1.
**3. Complementary events.** `P(E) + P(not E) = 1`. When “not E” is easier to count, compute that instead.

**4. Standard totals to memorise.** One die: 6 outcomes. Two dice: 36 outcomes. A well-shuffled deck: 52 cards, 26 red and 26 black, 4 of each rank, 12 face cards (J, Q, K of each suit) and 4 aces. A coin: 2 outcomes; two coins: 4.
**5. “At least one” questions** are nearly always fastest as `1 − P(none)`.
formulas: Deck: 52 cards, 26 red, 12 face cards, 4 aces
tricks: - **Always write the total number of outcomes first.** Half of all probability errors are wrong totals, not wrong favourable counts.
- For two dice, list the pairs systematically (1,1) to (6,6) when the condition is unusual, such as “sum is a prime number”.
- “Face card” means Jack, Queen or King — **not** the ace. Twelve face cards in a deck.
- A red king is 2 in a deck; a black face card is 6.
- “At least one” → use 1 − P(none). “At most” → count directly, it is usually short.
mistakes: - Forgetting that a die has 6 outcomes, not 6 faces times something — and that **two** dice have 36, not 12.
- Counting an ace as a face card.
- Simplifying the fraction incorrectly, or leaving it unsimplified when the answer is expected as a fraction.
- Writing a probability greater than 1. If that happens, your total is wrong.

qa.q: A card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck. What is the probability that it is a red king?
qa.a: There are 2 red kings, so P = 2/52 = 1/26.

qa.q: A die is thrown once. Find the probability of getting (i) a prime number, (ii) a number greater than 4.
a: Primes on a die are 2, 3, 5, so P = 3/6 = 1/2.
Numbers greater than 4 are 5 and 6, so P = 2/6 = 1/3.

qa.q: A bag contains 5 red and 3 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is not red.
qa.a: Total outcomes = 5 + 3 = 8. Not red means green, so P(not red) = 3/8. Equivalently, using the complement rule: P(not red) = 1 − P(red) = 1 − 5/8 = **3/8**. The complement route is quicker when the event you are asked about has more outcomes than the one you are not.

qa.q: A bag contains 4 red, 5 blue and 3 green balls. Find the probability of drawing a ball that is not green.
qa.a: Total balls = 12. Balls that are not green = 4 + 5 = 9. So P(not green) = 9/12 = 3/4.

qa.q: Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that the sum is 9.
A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck. Find the probability that it is (i) a face card, (ii) neither a king nor a red card.
a: (i) There are 12 face cards, so P = 12/52 = 3/13.
(ii) Red cards are 26, of which 2 are kings. Neither a king nor red means a black card that is not a king: 26 − 2 = 24.

qa.q: A student says, “Two dice are thrown, so there are 6 + 6 = 12 outcomes and P(sum = 7) = 6/12 = 1/2.” Find the error and give the correct probability.
a: Error: each die has 6 outcomes, so two dice have 6 × 6 = **36** outcomes, not 12.
Favourable outcomes for a sum of 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — 6 outcomes.

qa.q: A die has the letters A, B, C, D, E, A on its six faces. It is thrown once. Find the probability of getting (i) the letter A and (ii) the letter D.
a: (i) The letter A appears on 2 faces, so P(A) = 2/6 = **1/3**.
(ii) The letter D appears on 1 face, so P(D) = **1/6**.

qa.q: Two coins are tossed together. Find the probability of getting (i) two heads, (ii) at least one tail, (iii) at most one head.
a: Sample space = {HH, HT, TH, TT}: 4 equally likely outcomes.
(i) Two heads: only HH, so P = 1/4.
(ii) At least one tail: HT, TH, TT, so P = 3/4.
(iii) At most one head: HT, TH, TT, so P = 3/4.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A bag contains 5 red, 8 white and 7 black balls. One ball is drawn at random.

(a) Find the probability that it is red.
(b) Find the probability that it is not white.
(c) Find the probability that it is black or white.

Read and answer:

In a school raffle, 200 tickets numbered 1 to 200 are sold and one ticket is drawn at random.

(a) What is the probability that the number is a multiple of 10?
(b) What is the probability that it is a perfect square?
(c) What is the probability that it is not a multiple of 5?
a: (a) Multiples of 10 up to 200: 20, so P = 20/200 = **1/10**.
(b) Perfect squares up to 200: 1², 2², …, 14² (14² = 196), so 14 of them and P = 14/200 = **7/100**.
(c) Multiples of 5: 40, so P(not a multiple of 5) = 1 − 40/200 = **4/5**.

qa.q: A box contains 90 discs numbered 1 to 90. One disc is drawn at random. Find the probability that it bears (i) a two-digit number, (ii) a number divisible by 5, (iii) a perfect square number.
a: (i) Two-digit numbers are 10 to 90, i.e. 81 discs, so P = 81/90 = 9/10.
(ii) Multiples of 5 from 5 to 90: 18 numbers, so P = 18/90 = 1/5.
(iii) Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81 — nine numbers, so P = 9/90 = 1/10.

qa.q: Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that (i) the sum is less than 5, (ii) the product of the numbers is 12, (iii) a doublet is obtained, (iv) the sum is a prime number.
a: The sample space has 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.

mcq.q: The probability of an impossible event is: (a) 1  (b) 0  (c) 1/2  (d) undefined
Two dice are thrown together. The total number of outcomes is: (a) 36  (b) 6  (c) 12  (d) 24
The number of face cards in a deck of 52 cards is: (a) 8  (b) 16  (c) 12  (d) 4
mcq.a: **(c) 12.** Jacks, queens and kings of four suits.

mcq.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. The probability that a ball drawn at random is not red is: (a) 2/5  (b) 4/6  (c) 1/6  (d) 3/5
mcq.a: **(d) 3/5.** Blue balls = 6 out of 10, so P(not red) = 6/10 = 3/5.

mcq.q: The probability of getting an even prime number in one throw of a die is: (a) 1/6  (b) 1/2  (c) 1/3  (d) 0
mcq.a: **(a) 1/6.** The only even prime is 2, which is one of the six equally likely outcomes.

mcq.q: In one throw of a die, the probability of getting a number less than 7 is: (a) 0  (b) 1/6  (c) 5/6  (d) 1
mcq.a: **(d) 1.** Every outcome 1–6 is less than 7, so it is a sure event.

mcq.q: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck. The probability of a black queen is: (a) 1/52  (b) 1/26  (c) 1/13  (d) 2/13
mcq.a: **(b) 1/26.** Two black queens out of 52 cards gives 2/52 = 1/26.

trend: One 2–3 mark question every year, nearly always a deck of cards or two dice. Card questions are the most common.
onepager: - P(E) = favourable / total, and P(E) + P(not E) = 1.
- Two dice = 36 outcomes. Deck = 52, red 26, face cards 12.
task: Throw two dice 36 times and record the sums. Compare the frequency of each sum with the theoretical probabilities — 7 should come up most often. Small samples will not match exactly, which is the point of the exercise.
steps: 1. Write the **sample space** — the complete list of equally likely outcomes — before computing anything. Most wrong answers here come from an incomplete list.
2. Count the **favourable outcomes** for the event, and form **P(E) = favourable / total**. Reduce the fraction.
3. For a 'not' or 'at least' question, use the **complement**: P(not E) = 1 − P(E). For two events, check whether they are mutually exclusive before adding probabilities.
4. Sanity-check the value: it must lie between **0 and 1**, and the probabilities of all possible outcomes must add to **1**. For cards, remember 52 total, 12 face cards, 4 suits of 13.
